title: Pressure Vessel RBI to API 510: Vessels, Columns, Exchangers
description: Risk-based inspection for pressure vessels, columns and heat exchangers to API 510: internal versus on-stream inspection, bundles and interval plans.
h1: Risk-based inspection for pressure vessels, columns and heat exchangers
intro: For inspection and reliability engineers who decide which vessels open at the next turnaround and which can be inspected from the outside while running. This page sets out what API 510 lets a risk-based assessment change, the conditions under which an on-stream inspection can replace an internal one, why a heat exchanger has to be split into shell, channel and bundle, how inspection methods are matched to each damage mechanism, and how Atlantis runs a vessel and exchanger RBI study remotely from your records.

highlights.h: Internal or on-stream, decided per vessel
highlights.p: Whether a vessel must be opened depends on what is damaging it and whether that damage can be measured from outside. The study answers that vessel by vessel, with the method and coverage an on-stream inspection would need to be a genuine substitute.

Shell, channel and tube bundle fail in different ways with different consequences. Treating an exchanger as one item hides the bundle that leaks every other run behind a shell that has barely corroded in twenty years of service.

The plan tells you which vessels need entry, which can be checked before the shutdown and which carry low enough risk to wait, with the reasoning written down for your inspector, your engineers and anyone who audits the decision later.

sections.h: What API 510 allows an RBI assessment to change
p: API 510 (eleventh edition, October 2022, with errata in 2023 and 2025) sets default limits for in-service vessels: the internal or on-stream inspection interval is the lesser of half the remaining life or 10 years, and the external visual interval is the lesser of five years or the internal or on-stream interval. Each of those limits applies unless a risk-based assessment justifies something different, and an RBI assessment can set the internal, on-stream and external intervals, including intervals beyond the default caps.

That freedom carries a condition. Where an RBI-based internal or on-stream interval runs past the 10-year limit, the code requires the RBI assessment itself to be reviewed and approved by the engineer and the inspector on a fixed maximum cycle, which was 10 years in the editions we reviewed, and sooner if process, equipment or consequence changes warrant it. A vessel interval that outlives its supporting assessment has lost its basis.

Vessels rarely stand alone in a study. Pressure relief devices protecting them can be brought into the same programme, since API RP 581 includes a method for relief devices, and the exchangers in the unit are usually assessed in the same workshops because they share the corrosion loops.

sections.h: When an on-stream inspection can replace an internal one
p: API 510 allows an on-stream inspection to substitute for the internal inspection when its conditions are met. In the version we checked, these include a general corrosion rate below 0.005 in/yr (0.125 mm/yr), a remaining life above 10 years, a corrosive character established by mild service or several years of comparable operation, no suspected environmental cracking or high-temperature hydrogen attack, no internal components or linings that would stop external scanning from seeing the damage, and the inspector's approval. Where the remaining life is 10 years or less, a narrower route exists if the service history is established, the examination can fully characterise the damage (for example high-density automated ultrasonic scanning) and both inspector and engineer approve. Confirm the clause wording in the edition you work to.

RBI adds the reasoning behind each substitution. For a vessel suffering general thinning that a corrosion map from outside can measure, on-stream inspection can earn the same effectiveness as entry. For one suffering cracking at internal attachment welds, localised attack under deposits, lining or cladding breakdown or tray damage, an external survey cannot see the threat and the plan keeps the internal inspection. sections.h: Heat exchangers: shell, channel and bundle
p: An exchanger is several items. The shell and the channel or head are pressure components assessed under API 510 like any vessel. The tube bundle is a replaceable component whose typical failure is a leak from one side to the other, which contaminates product, upsets the process or forces an unplanned shutdown more often than it releases fluid to atmosphere. Splitting the exchanger lets each part be inspected on its own logic.

API RP 581 includes a method for exchanger bundles that draws on the failure history of the bundle and of similar bundles in comparable service, and frames consequence largely in production and repair terms. Even where the owner does not run that method, the same thinking applies: record each bundle's install date, tube material, plugging history and inspection results, and the bundle's own risk becomes visible instead of sitting inside the shell's.

Tube inspection is specified by method and sample. Eddy current testing suits non-ferrous tubes, internal rotary inspection (IRIS) gives measured wall thickness in ferrous and non-ferrous tubes, and remote field or near-field methods screen ferrous tubes. The plan states the percentage of tubes, how they are selected (a random sample plus the rows that history says fail first, such as the inlet pass) and what result triggers a larger sample, a plugging campaign or a retube.

sections.h: Records a vessel and exchanger study needs
p: Vessel studies lean heavily on construction records, because material, heat treatment and design margin decide which mechanisms are credible. The request covers:
list: Manufacturer's data reports or equivalent, nameplate data, general arrangement drawings, material specifications, post-weld heat treatment records and minimum design metal temperature.
Design and operating pressure and temperature, including start-up, shutdown and upset conditions.
Internals and linings: trays, packing, demisters, cladding, weld overlay, refractory and internal coatings.
Inspection history: internal, external and on-stream reports with thickness data, corrosion maps and crack examination results.
Repairs, alterations and rerates, with the drawings and calculations that went with them.
Process chemistry and integrity operating windows, with records of exceedances.
For exchangers: tube material and gauge, tube inspection reports, plugging maps, bundle replacement history and cleaning practice.
Consequence inputs: inventory, phase, toxicity (hydrogen sulfide, hydrofluoric acid), location in the unit and what a forced outage would stop.

sections.h: Matching inspection effectiveness to the damage mechanism
p: Inspection effectiveness is specific to a mechanism. A thickness survey that rates as highly effective against general thinning may be close to useless against wet hydrogen sulfide cracking, and the plan has to reflect that rather than reusing one grade for every mechanism on the vessel. The study pairs each credible mechanism with methods that can actually find it:
list: General and local thinning: ultrasonic thickness readings at representative points for slow general loss, corrosion mapping for local attack and under-deposit pitting.
Surface-breaking cracking (amine, caustic, sulfide stress, chloride): wet fluorescent magnetic particle or penetrant examination of prepared weld surfaces, usually from inside.
Embedded or subsurface cracking and high-temperature hydrogen attack: advanced ultrasonic techniques qualified for the damage, applied where the screening says they are needed.
Lining, cladding and overlay breakdown: internal visual examination with targeted thickness or ferrite checks.
External corrosion and corrosion under insulation or fireproofing: visual survey, insulation removal at chosen points and screening methods suited to the geometry.

p: Atlantis carries out the study remotely. Records come through a shared data room, each unit is reviewed in video workshops with its process, corrosion and inspection specialists, and the draft risk ranking is circulated before the inspection plan is written so that disagreements about mechanisms are settled early. Where turnaround scope has to be frozen by a set date, we plan the study back from that date and say at the outset what can be achieved with the data available.

Physical checks stay with your own inspectors: confirming nameplates, internals and insulation condition, and locating heat treatment records that only exist on paper in the plant. In the United States, Atlantis can also send UT, MT, PT and VT technicians to close specific gaps, for example a corrosion map on a vessel with no thickness history or magnetic particle examination of welds the study flags. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States.

sections.h: What the vessel and exchanger plan delivers
p: For every vessel, exchanger shell and channel, and bundle, the plan sets out:
list: Risk category with the probability and consequence drivers named.
Inspection type (internal, on-stream or external) and the justification where on-stream replaces internal.
Next due date with its basis and the API 510 default date shown alongside.
Method, coverage and surface preparation for each credible mechanism.
For bundles: tube inspection method, sample size, selection rule and the results that would trigger action.
Relief device intervals where devices are in scope.
Assumptions, data gaps and reassessment triggers.

sections.h: Using the assessment to set turnaround scope
p: Risk-based planning earns its keep before a turnaround. The assessment identifies vessels that must be entered, vessels whose inspection can be done on-stream in the months before the shutdown so that they drop out of the critical path, and vessels whose risk is low enough to defer within code limits and with approval. Bundles are scheduled for pulling on the basis of their own risk rather than the shell's due date.

When the shutdown inspection finds damage, your inspector evaluates it against the code and your engineer decides on continued operation; any fitness-for-service assessment stays with your engineer, because Atlantis does not perform that work. The findings and measured rates then go back into the assessment so the post-turnaround plan rests on what was actually seen.
Reviews of existing vessel programmes keep turning up the same problems:
list: Thickness readings credited against cracking mechanisms they cannot detect.
Post-weld heat treatment status assumed rather than taken from records, which changes the answer for amine and caustic cracking.
Exchangers carried as a single item, so bundle failures never shape the plan.
On-stream inspection accepted as equivalent to entry for vessels whose internals hide the damage.
Relief devices left out, although they protect every vessel in the study.
The assessment not updated after a rerate or change of service, leaving the interval tied to conditions that no longer exist.

faqs.q: Can RBI take an API 510 internal inspection beyond 10 years?
faqs.a: Yes, if the assessment justifies it. API 510 allows an RBI assessment to set internal and on-stream intervals beyond the default of half the remaining life or 10 years. When it does, the code requires the RBI assessment to be reviewed and approved by the engineer and the inspector on a fixed cycle, and sooner if process, equipment or consequence changes. Your inspector approves the resulting interval.

faqs.q: When can an on-stream inspection replace an internal inspection?
faqs.a: When the API 510 conditions are met: in the version we checked, a low and established general corrosion rate, a remaining life above 10 years, no suspected environmental cracking or high-temperature hydrogen attack, internals that do not prevent external scanning, and the inspector's approval. The RBI study shows, vessel by vessel, whether the external method can actually find the active damage.

faqs.q: How are heat exchanger bundles handled in RBI?
faqs.a: As their own items. A bundle's failure is usually a leak between shell and tube sides, with consequences in contamination and lost production. API RP 581 has a bundle method based on failure history of the bundle and similar bundles. The plan sets the tube inspection method, sample size and selection, and the results that would trigger a larger sample, plugging or retubing.

faqs.q: Does the vessel study include pressure relief devices?
faqs.a: It can. Relief devices protect every vessel in the study, and API RP 581 includes a method for setting their test intervals from the risk of a device failing to open or leaking. Where devices are in scope, the plan gives an interval for each with its basis. Where they are not, the report notes that relief device intervals continue under your existing programme.

faqs.q: Why don't thickness readings count for a vessel in wet hydrogen sulfide service?
faqs.a: Because the threats in that service are blistering and cracking, and a thickness survey is not designed to find cracks. Inspection credit is specific to each mechanism, so a vessel can have excellent thickness history and still carry a high cracking probability. The plan specifies crack-detection examination of the welds and susceptible zones instead.

faqs.q: Can the study be ready before our turnaround scope freeze?
faqs.a: That depends mainly on how quickly the records can be gathered. We plan the study back from your scope freeze date, agree the data request and workshop dates at the outset, and say early on what can be achieved with the data available. Where records are missing, the study flags those vessels so that the scope decision is taken knowingly rather than by default.

faqs.q: What if manufacturer's data reports are missing?
faqs.a: Material, thickness and heat treatment can sometimes be recovered from purchase records, drawings, previous inspection reports or field verification such as positive material identification and hardness checks. Where they cannot, the study uses conservative assumptions, states them, and the plan asks for the verification that would remove the assumption.

faqs.q: Who approves the vessel inspection intervals?
faqs.a: Your API 510 inspector, together with your engineer where the code requires it, or the inspection authority your company procedure names. Atlantis prepares the assessment and the proposed plan and explains the reasoning, but approval and the vessel's inspection record stay with your organisation.

API 510 on-stream in lieu of internal conditions: corrosion rate < 0.005 in/yr (0.125 mm/yr), remaining life > 10 years, established service, no suspected environmental cracking or HTHA, no internals preventing external scanning, inspector approval; alternative for RL <= 10 years with established history, accurate NDE such as high-density AUT, inspector and engineer approval (edition not named by the source)

API 510 default intervals (lesser of RL/2 or 10 years internal/on-stream; lesser of 5 years or internal interval external) unless RBI justifies otherwise; RBI assessment reviewed and approved by engineer and inspector on a maximum cycle (10 years in editions reviewed) when RBI intervals exceed 10 years; API RP 581 4th ed. covers PRDs and exchanger bundles (already on the site)
